title: Organize Complex Information Around One Decision
subtitle: Give the main path a small set of labeled parts and keep supporting detail easy to retrieve.
description: Define the audience and decision, group related material into labeled parts, put the main path in a useful order, and move supporting detail into linked layers instead of either flattening everything or presenting every detail at once.

lifeOsSource.hack: Structure complex material around the audience's immediate task, then separate the main path from supporting detail without deleting the detail that may still matter.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Name the primary audience and the decision or action they need to understand. Group related material by purpose, give each group a descriptive label, order the groups into a main path, and move supporting definitions, examples, calculations or source detail into a layer that remains easy to retrieve.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What does the audience need to decide or do, which groups form the main path, what belongs in supporting detail, and can a reader find that detail when needed?

faq.question: How many groups should I create?
faq.answer: Use the smallest set that preserves the distinctions the audience needs. If a group mixes unrelated purposes, split it. If several groups can be understood and used as one, combine them. The structure should follow the material rather than a universal count.

faq.question: What if I have several audiences?
faq.answer: Keep one stable underlying source and create different main paths when the audiences need different decisions or levels of detail. Do not force every audience through the same summary merely to avoid maintaining separate views.
faq.answerHtml: Keep one stable underlying source and create different main paths when the audiences need different decisions or levels of detail. Do not force every audience through the same summary merely to avoid maintaining separate views.

faq.question: What should move out of the main path?
faq.answer: Move material that is useful for verification, implementation or deeper understanding but is not required to follow the immediate decision. Keep links or labels clear enough that the detail is not lost.

intro.html: Complex information becomes difficult to use when every detail competes for the same level of attention. The alternative is not to delete nuance. Build a main path around the audience's immediate decision or action, then preserve definitions, examples, calculations and deeper context in labeled supporting layers.

sections.title: 1. Define the audience and immediate task
sections.html: State who needs the information and what they need to understand, decide, explain or do next. Use that task to distinguish essential context from material that can remain available without occupying the main path.

sections.title: 2. Group material by purpose
sections.html: Put related facts, constraints, steps, definitions or examples together and give each group a descriptive label. A useful label tells the reader what role the group plays rather than merely repeating a section number.

sections.title: 3. Build the main path
sections.html: Order the labeled groups so the audience can move from context to the important distinction and then to the decision or next action. Remove duplicate explanations from the main path, but keep necessary caveats where removing them would change the meaning.

sections.title: 4. Preserve supporting layers
sections.html: Place deeper detail in appendices, linked notes, expandable sections, source references or separate technical views. Make the connection to the main path explicit so a reader can inspect the detail without having to search the entire source again.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace unsupported working-memory and comprehension claims, fabricated internal outcomes, universal chunk counts, fixed timing and word limits and pseudo-precise audience or template multipliers with a bounded information-structure workflow.
